items.stem: What is a budget deficit?
options: Government spending exceeds tax revenue in a year
items.answer: Government spending exceeds tax revenue in a year
items.markingKey: Flow; financed by borrowing.

items.stem: Explain the difference between a budget deficit and the national debt.
items.answer: A budget deficit is a flow: the shortfall of revenue below spending in one year. The national debt is a stock: the total accumulated borrowing that has not been repaid.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Explain why a government might choose to run a budget deficit.
items.answer: To boost AD in a recession; to finance investment in infrastructure that raises future growth; to smooth taxes over the cycle.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each reason explained [2]

items.stem: In Tarvia, government spending is $220bn, tax revenue is $210bn and GDP is $400bn. The national debt at the start of the year is $600bn. Calculate the budget balance as a percentage of GDP.

In Jovania, government spending is $250bn, tax revenue is $160bn and GDP is $500bn. The national debt at the start of the year is $600bn. (a) Calculate the budget balance and state whether it is a deficit or surplus. (b) Calculate the national debt at the end of the year and as a percentage of GDP. (c) Explain one reason why the debt-to-GDP ratio might fall even if the government runs a deficit.
items.answer: (a) −$90bn: deficit. (b) $690bn; 138% of GDP. (c) If nominal GDP grows faster than the debt (through real growth and inflation), the ratio falls.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) debt [1]; ratio [1] (c) GDP growth reason [1] [4]

items.stem: Extract: After a deep recession, the budget deficit in Korvia rose from 3% to 8% of GDP and national debt from 60% to 85% of GDP. Part of the rise was caused by automatic stabilisers; the rest by a discretionary programme of infrastructure spending and a temporary cut in VAT. The opposition calls for immediate spending cuts. (a) Explain the difference between the budget deficit and the national debt. (b) Explain how automatic stabilisers increased the deficit.
items.answer: (a) Deficit = annual flow; debt = accumulated stock. (b) Lower incomes reduced tax revenue; higher unemployment raised benefit spending.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Deficit = annual flow; debt = accumulated stock. [2] (b) Credit: Lower incomes reduced tax revenue; higher unemployment raised benefit spending. [2]

items.stem: The national debt of Kestria has risen to 110% of GDP. Explain two possible problems this could cause.
items.answer: High interest payments (opportunity cost); higher interest rates/crowding out; loss of confidence; future tax rises; less room for fiscal stimulus.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: In Korvia, government spending is $250bn, tax revenue is $190bn and GDP is $400bn. The national debt at the start of the year is $200bn. Calculate the budget balance as a percentage of GDP.
Which is a direct tax?
items.answer: Income tax
items.markingKey: Levied on income/wealth, paid directly by the taxpayer.

items.stem: Explain the difference between direct and indirect taxes, with an example of each.
items.answer: Direct taxes are levied on income or wealth and paid by the person taxed (income tax, corporation tax). Indirect taxes are levied on spending and collected by sellers (VAT, excise duties).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each with example [2]

items.stem: Explain why an indirect tax can be regressive even if every consumer pays the same rate.
items.answer: Low-income households spend a larger proportion of their income, so the tax takes a larger share of their income than of high-income households.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: spending share; 1 mark: tax/income higher for poor [2]

items.stem: A sales tax of 15% is charged on all goods in Nordavia. How is this tax best described?
items.answer: Regressive tax
items.markingKey: Regressive tax: it takes a higher proportion of the income of the poor, who spend more of their income.

items.stem: A tax on company profits in Umbria Nova is set at 25% for all firms. How is this tax best described? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Proportional tax: same rate on profits of all sizes.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Proportional tax; 1 mark: explanation – same rate on profits of all sizes. [2]

items.stem: Classify each tax and explain. (i) Every adult in Bangkok pays the same $300 a year local tax. (ii) Every worker in Fendaria pays 20% of income in tax regardless of income.
items.answer: (i) Regressive tax (ii) Proportional tax
items.markingKey: (i) Regressive tax – a fixed amount is a larger share of a low income. [2] (ii) Proportional tax – the same proportion of income for all. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: Extract: After a deep recession, the budget deficit in Jovania rose from 2% to 7% of GDP and national debt from 60% to 85% of GDP. Part of the rise was caused by automatic stabilisers; the rest by a discretionary programme of infrastructure spending and a temporary cut in VAT. The opposition calls for immediate spending cuts. (a) Explain the difference between the budget deficit and the national debt. (b) Explain how automatic stabilisers increased the deficit.
items.answer: (a) Deficit = annual flow; debt = accumulated stock. (b) Lower incomes reduced tax revenue; higher unemployment raised benefit spending.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Deficit = annual flow; debt = accumulated stock. [2] (b) Credit: Lower incomes reduced tax revenue; higher unemployment raised benefit spending. [2]

items.stem: Extract: After a deep recession, the budget deficit in Sundara rose from 3% to 8% of GDP and national debt from 70% to 95% of GDP. Part of the rise was caused by automatic stabilisers; the rest by a discretionary programme of infrastructure spending and a temporary cut in VAT. The opposition calls for immediate spending cuts. (a) Explain the difference between the budget deficit and the national debt. (b) Explain how the VAT cut and infrastructure spending were intended to affect AD.
items.answer: (a) Deficit = annual flow; debt = accumulated stock. (b) Higher disposable income/consumption and higher G raise AD, output and employment.
items.markingKey: (a) Credit: Deficit = annual flow; debt = accumulated stock. [2] (b) Credit: Higher disposable income/consumption and higher G raise AD, output and employment. [3]

items.stem: Which is an indirect tax?
options: Value added tax on goods and services
items.answer: Value added tax on goods and services
items.markingKey: Levied on spending.

items.stem: Which is an example of expansionary fiscal policy?
items.answer: A cut in income tax
items.markingKey: Raises AD.

items.stem: Explain how expansionary fiscal policy can reduce unemployment.
items.answer: Higher government spending or lower taxes raise AD; firms increase output to meet demand and hire more workers, reducing cyclical unemployment.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: AD rises; 1 mark: output and employment rise [2]

items.stem: Explain two limitations of using fiscal policy to manage AD.
items.answer: Time lags; budget deficits and debt; crowding out of private spending; leakages into imports and saving; inflation if near capacity; political pressures.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each, 1 mark each explained [4]

items.stem: The government of Merania cuts income tax rates. Is this expansionary or contractionary fiscal policy?
items.answer: Expansionary fiscal policy
items.markingKey: Expansionary fiscal policy: higher disposable income raises consumption and AD.

items.stem: The government of Marvona raises VAT from 15% to 20%. Is this expansionary or contractionary fiscal policy? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Contractionary fiscal policy: higher taxes reduce real disposable income and AD.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Contractionary fiscal policy; 1 mark: explanation – higher taxes reduce real disposable income and AD. [2]

items.stem: Classify each measure and explain its effect on AD. (i) The government of Korvia abolishes a tax allowance, raising income tax bills. (ii) The government of Korvia increases unemployment benefits.
items.answer: (i) Contractionary fiscal policy (ii) Expansionary fiscal policy
items.markingKey: (i) Contractionary fiscal policy – lower disposable income. [2] (ii) Expansionary fiscal policy – higher transfers raise disposable income and consumption. [2] Total [4]

items.stem: What is an automatic stabiliser?
options: A rule that fixes interest rates
A deliberate change in tax rates
A form of spending or taxation that changes with the economic cycle without government action
items.answer: A form of spending or taxation that changes with the economic cycle without government action
items.markingKey: e.g. progressive taxes, unemployment benefits.

items.stem: Explain how progressive income taxes act as an automatic stabiliser.
items.answer: In a boom incomes rise and people move into higher bands, so tax takes a rising share and dampens spending; in a recession tax falls faster than income, supporting spending.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: boom; 1 mark: recession [2]

items.stem: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of discretionary fiscal policy.
items.answer: Advantage: can be large and targeted at specific problems. Disadvantage: time lags in recognising, deciding and implementing; political motives; may be mistimed.
items.markingKey: 1 mark each [2]

items.stem: Unemployment benefit payments in Esteria rise as more people lose their jobs. Is this an automatic stabiliser or discretionary fiscal policy?
items.answer: Automatic stabiliser
items.markingKey: Automatic stabiliser: spending rises automatically in a downturn.

items.stem: The government of Istrana announces a new $20bn road-building programme to fight a recession. Is this an automatic stabiliser or discretionary fiscal policy? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Discretionary fiscal policy: a deliberate policy decision.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Discretionary fiscal policy; 1 mark: explanation – a deliberate policy decision. [2]

items.stem: The government of Nordavia has asked its economic advisers for a report on this issue. (a) Explain the differences between direct and indirect taxes and between progressive, regressive and proportional taxes. items.stem: Tax revenue in Pelora falls automatically as incomes fall in a recession. Is this an automatic stabiliser or discretionary fiscal policy?
items.answer: Automatic stabiliser
items.markingKey: Automatic stabiliser: revenue changes with the cycle without a policy decision.

items.stem: Extract: After a deep recession, the budget deficit in Rovania rose from 2% to 7% of GDP and national debt from 70% to 95% of GDP. Part of the rise was caused by automatic stabilisers; the rest by a discretionary programme of infrastructure spending and a temporary cut in VAT. The opposition calls for immediate spending cuts. (a) Calculate the increase in the debt-to-GDP ratio in percentage points. (b) Explain the difference between the budget deficit and the national debt. (c) Explain how automatic stabilisers increased the deficit. (d) Explain how the VAT cut and infrastructure spending were intended to affect AD.
items.answer: (a) 25 percentage points (b) Deficit = annual flow; debt = accumulated stock. (c) Lower incomes reduced tax revenue; higher unemployment raised benefit spending. (d) Higher disposable income/consumption and higher G raise AD, output and employment.
